paragraphs: As she came into the room, Grushenka glanced only for an instant at Mitya, who looked at her uneasily. But her face reassured him at once. After the usual first questions and warnings, Nikolay Parfenovitch asked her, hesitating a little but keeping up his most courteous manner, what her relationship was with the retired lieutenant, Dmitri Fyodorovitch Karamazov. Grushenka answered firmly and quietly:

“He was an acquaintance. He came to see me as an acquaintance during the last month.” To further prying questions she answered plainly and with complete frankness. She said that “at times” she had thought him attractive, but that she had not loved him. She had won his heart, and his old father’s too, “out of my own nasty spite.” She had seen that Mitya was very jealous of Fyodor Pavlovitch and of everyone else, but that had only amused her. She had never meant to go to Fyodor Pavlovitch; she had simply been laughing at him. “I had no thoughts for either of them all this last month. I was expecting another man, who had wronged me. But I think,” she said in conclusion, “that there’s no need for you to ask about that, or for me to answer you, because that’s my own affair.”

Nikolay Parfenovitch took the hint at once. Again he dropped the “romantic” side of the case and moved on to the serious one, the question of most importance, the three thousand roubles. Grushenka confirmed that three thousand roubles had certainly been spent on the first carousal at Mokroe. She had not counted the money herself, but she had heard from Dmitri Fyodorovitch’s own lips that it was three thousand.
“Did he tell you that when you were alone, or in front of someone else? Or did you only hear him speak of it to others in your presence?” the prosecutor asked at once.
Grushenka replied that she had heard him say it in front of other people, and had heard him say it when they were alone.
“Did he say it to you alone once, or several times?” asked the prosecutor, and learned that he had told Grushenka so several times.

Ippolit Kirillovitch was very well satisfied with this piece of evidence. Further questioning brought out that Grushenka also knew where that money had come from, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had got it from Katerina Ivanovna.
“And did you never, not once, hear that the money spent a month ago was not three thousand but less, and that Dmitri Fyodorovitch had saved half of it for his own use?”
“No, I never heard that,” answered Grushenka.
It was explained further that Mitya had, on the contrary, often told her that he hadn’t a farthing.
“He was always expecting to get some from his father,” said Grushenka in conclusion.
“Did he ever say in your presence ... casually, or in a moment of irritation,” Nikolay Parfenovitch put in suddenly, “that he intended to make an attempt on his father’s life?”
“Ach, he did say so,” sighed Grushenka.
“Once or several times?”
“He mentioned it several times, always in anger.”
“And did you believe he would do it?”
“No, I never believed it,” she answered firmly. “I had faith in his noble heart.”
“Gentlemen, allow me,” Mitya cried suddenly, “allow me to say one word to Agrafena Alexandrovna, in your presence.”
“You may speak,” Nikolay Parfenovitch agreed.
“Agrafena Alexandrovna!” Mitya got up from his chair. “Have faith in God and in me. I am not guilty of my father’s murder!”

Having said these words, Mitya sat down again. Grushenka stood up and crossed herself devoutly before the icon. “Thanks be to You, O Lord,” she said in a voice trembling with emotion. Still standing, she turned to Nikolay Parfenovitch and added:

“Believe it, now that he has spoken like that! I know him. He’ll say anything as a joke or out of stubbornness, but he’ll never deceive you against his conscience. He’s telling the whole truth, you can believe it.”
“Thank you, Agrafena Alexandrovna, you’ve given me fresh courage,” Mitya answered in a quivering voice.

As for the money spent the day before, she declared that she did not know what sum it was, but she had heard him tell several people that he had three thousand with him. And when asked where he got the money, she said he had told her he had “stolen” it from Katerina Ivanovna. She had answered that he had not stolen it, and that he must pay the money back next day. The prosecutor asked her emphatically whether the money he said he had stolen from Katerina Ivanovna was what he had spent yesterday or what he had squandered here a month ago. She declared that he meant the money spent a month ago, and that this was how she understood him.

Grushenka was at last released. Nikolay Parfenovitch told her, on an impulse, that she could return to the town at once, and that if he could help her in any way, with horses for example, or if she would like an escort, he ... would be—

“I thank you sincerely,” said Grushenka, bowing to him. “I’m going with this old gentleman, I’m driving him back to town with me. Meanwhile, if you’ll allow me, I’ll wait downstairs to hear what you decide about Dmitri Fyodorovitch.”

She went out. Mitya was calm and even looked more cheerful, but only for a moment. He felt more and more weighed down by a strange physical weakness. His eyes were closing with fatigue. The examination of the witnesses was finally over. They went on to a final revision of the protocol. Mitya got up and moved from his chair to the corner by the curtain. He lay down on a large chest covered with a rug and fell asleep instantly.
He had a strange dream, utterly out of keeping with the place and the time.

He was driving somewhere in the steppes, where he had been stationed long ago, and a peasant was driving him in a cart with a pair of horses, through snow and sleet. He was cold. It was early in November, and the snow was falling in big wet flakes that melted as soon as they touched the ground. The peasant drove him briskly. He had a fair, long beard. He was not an old man, about fifty, and he wore a gray peasant’s smock. Not far off was a village. He could see the black huts, and half of them were burnt down, with only the charred beams sticking up. As they drove in, there were peasant women lined up along the road, a lot of women, a whole row of them, all thin and wan, their faces a sort of brownish color. One stood at the edge, a tall, bony woman who looked forty but might have been only twenty, with a long thin face. In her arms was a little baby, crying. Her breasts seemed so dried up that there was not a drop of milk in them. The child cried and cried and held out its little bare arms, its little fists blue with cold.
“Why are they crying? Why are they crying?” Mitya asked, as they dashed gaily by.
“It’s the babe,” answered the driver. “The babe weeping.”
And Mitya was struck that he said, in his peasant way, “the babe,” and he liked the peasant calling it a “babe.” There seemed to be more pity in it.
“But why is it weeping?” Mitya persisted stupidly. “Why are its little arms bare? Why don’t they wrap it up?”
“The babe’s cold. Its little clothes are frozen and don’t warm it.”
“But why is it like that? Why?” foolish Mitya still persisted.
“Why, they’re poor people, burnt out. They’ve no bread. They’re begging because they’ve been burnt out.”

“No, no,” said Mitya, as if he still did not understand. “Tell me why those poor mothers stand there. Why are people poor? Why is the babe poor? Why is the steppe barren? Why don’t they hug each other and kiss? Why don’t they sing songs of joy? Why are they so dark from black misery? Why don’t they feed the babe?”

And he felt that, though his questions were unreasonable and senseless, he still wanted to ask just that, and he had to ask it just that way. He felt a passion of pity rising in his heart, such as he had never known before. He wanted to cry. He wanted to do something for them all, so that the babe should weep no more, so that the dark-faced, dried-up mother should not weep, so that no one should shed tears again from that moment on. And he wanted to do it at once, at once, regardless of all obstacles, with all the recklessness of the Karamazovs.

“And I’m coming with you. I won’t leave you now for the rest of my life, I’m coming with you,” he heard Grushenka’s tender voice close beside him, trembling with emotion. And his heart glowed, and he struggled forward toward the light, and he longed to live, to live, to go on and on, toward the new, beckoning light, and to hurry, hurry, now, at once!

“What! Where?” he exclaimed, opening his eyes and sitting up on the chest, smiling brightly, as though he had come back from a faint. Nikolay Parfenovitch was standing over him, suggesting that he listen to the protocol being read aloud and sign it. Mitya guessed that he had been asleep an hour or more, but he did not hear Nikolay Parfenovitch. He was suddenly struck by the fact that there was a pillow under his head, which had not been there when he had leaned back, exhausted, on the chest.
“Who put that pillow under my head? Who was so kind?” he cried, with a sort of ecstatic gratitude and tears in his voice, as though some great kindness had been shown him.

He never found out who this kind man was. Perhaps one of the peasant witnesses, or Nikolay Parfenovitch’s little secretary, had thought compassionately to put a pillow under his head. But his whole soul was quivering with tears. He went to the table and said that he would sign whatever they liked.
“I’ve had a good dream, gentlemen,” he said in a strange voice, with a new light, as of joy, in his face.
